chapter.title: Buying the whole bazaar at once

cards.body: What if you skipped choosing a shop and bought a slice of all 50 of the bazaar's biggest ones, for ₹500 a month? That's an **index fund**: one basket holding every shop on the Nifty 50 board. Nobody inside it is guessing which stall wins next. The list decides.
cards.simpler: Picture skipping the job of choosing one shop. Instead, for ₹500 a month, you buy a small slice of all 50 of the biggest shops in the bazaar. That's an **index fund**: one basket that holds every shop on the Nifty 50 board. No one inside is guessing which stall will do best next. The list makes the choice.

cards.prompt: Two shoppers offer to fill your bazaar basket. A just copies the Nifty 50 list. B tastes samosas at every stall and reads the ledgers before picking. Who charges you less each year?

options.text: Same: a shopper is a shopper

whyNot.b: That's the effort, not the price: tasting and reading is work, and you pay for it.
whyNot.c: That's the job title, not the bill: copying a list takes far less work than picking.

cards.reteach: Copying a list needs no research team. Picking does, and that cost comes out of your money every year.

cards.title: Copy the list or pay a picker
cards.body:
An *index fund* is a mutual fund with the Nifty 50 list taped to its basket. It buys every shop on the list, bigger shops in bigger slices. When the list changes, the basket changes. No opinions needed.

An *active mutual fund* pays a manager to pick the stalls they think will beat the list. You pay for that judgment through the *expense ratio*: the yearly percentage of your money the fund keeps to run itself.

You'd think paying an expert gets you more. John Bogle spent his career arguing the reverse: **after fees, most pickers end up behind the plain list**, and the list costs almost nothing to copy.
cards.simpler: An index fund copies the Nifty 50 list. It buys every shop on it, with bigger slices of bigger shops, and changes when the list changes. An active fund pays a manager to pick stalls they hope will beat the list. You pay for that through the expense ratio, the share of your money the fund keeps each year. John Bogle argued **after fees, most pickers end up behind the plain list**, which costs almost nothing to copy.

cards.title: Meera's two baskets
cards.body: Meera has ₹1 lakh. Basket one, a Nifty 50 index fund, charges 0.2% a year (₹200 to start), and basket two, an active fund, charges 1.5% (₹1,500). Say both grow 10% a year before fees. After 20 years the index fund holds about ₹6.5 lakh and the active fund about ₹5.1 lakh. So **a 1.3% gap in fees became a ₹1.4 lakh gap in money**, and Meera never got a single bill for it.
cards.simpler: Meera has ₹1 lakh. She compares two baskets. A Nifty 50 index fund charges 0.2% a year, which is ₹200 to start. An active fund charges 1.5%, or ₹1,500. Say both grow 10% a year before fees. After 20 years, the index fund holds about ₹6.5 lakh and the active fund about ₹5.1 lakh. So **a 1.3% gap in fees became a ₹1.4 lakh gap in money**, and she never got a bill for it.

cards.prompt: Two Nifty 50 index funds, same 50 shops. Fund X charges 0.18% a year. Fund Y charges 0.45% and has a shinier logo. You'll put in ₹2,000 a month for years. Which do you pick?

options.text: Fund Y: a higher fee means better care
Fund X: same shops, smaller cut
Either: under 1% is too small to matter

whyNot.a: That's how you'd think about a picker, not a copier: both funds copy one list, so there's nothing extra to care for.
whyNot.c: That's one year's view, not twenty's: the cut repeats every year on a growing pile, as Meera found.

cards.reteach: Two funds copying one list hold the same shops and move almost together. The only real difference is the fee, so take the smaller one.

cards.title: Set it, then check the cut
cards.body:
A *SIP* (systematic investment plan) is a standing order: the same amount leaves your bank on the same date every month and buys units, which are slices of the fund. Say ₹1,000 on the 5th, with no decision needed. When prices are low it buys more units, and when they're high it buys fewer.

The expense ratio never arrives as a bill. It is taken out of the fund's value a little each day, like a slow drip from a rooftop water tank you never climb up to check.

Every fund also comes as a *Direct* or a *Regular* plan. **Regular pays a middleman's commission, so choose Direct**: same shops, lower fee.
cards.simpler: A SIP (systematic investment plan) takes the same amount, say ₹1,000, from your bank on the 5th of every month and buys units, which are slices of the fund. Low prices buy more units; high prices buy fewer. The expense ratio never comes as a bill. It drips out of the fund's value a little each day. Every fund comes as Direct or Regular. **Regular pays a middleman's commission, so choose Direct**: same shops, lower fee.

cards.body: Karan opens his app, taps the fund with the biggest one-year return, and starts a ₹3,000 SIP. It's an active fund on a Regular plan charging 1.6% a year, and he never notices, because no bill ever comes. **The fee hides, so you have to go looking for it.** To spot it, open the fund page, find 'expense ratio', and check that the fund name includes 'Direct'.
cards.simpler: Karan opens his app, taps the fund with the biggest one-year return, and starts a ₹3,000 SIP. It's an active fund on a Regular plan that charges 1.6% a year. He never notices, because no bill ever comes. **The fee hides, so you have to go looking for it.** To find it, open the fund page, look for 'expense ratio', and check that the fund name says 'Direct'.

cards.prompt: Your Nifty 50 index fund page says: Expense ratio 0.20%. You have ₹10,000 in it. What does that number mean?

options.text: About ₹20 a year, taken quietly from the fund's value
The fund promises to beat Nifty by 0.20% a year
A one-time ₹20 fee when your SIP starts

whyNot.b: That's a return, not a fee: an index fund aims to match Nifty, minus this cost.
whyNot.c: That's a one-off charge, not a yearly one: this cut repeats every year you hold the fund.

cards.reteach: The expense ratio is a yearly cut of what you hold. 0.20% of ₹10,000 is ₹20, taken every year and already subtracted from the fund's price.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body:
An index fund buys a slice of all 50 Nifty shops with no one picking, so its yearly fee, the expense ratio, stays tiny. **Set a monthly SIP in a Direct plan, and check that one fee number before anything else.**

Tomorrow: the tax on selling, and why a few extra months can shrink it.
cards.simpler:
An index fund buys a slice of all 50 Nifty shops, and no one picks, so its yearly fee, the expense ratio, stays tiny. **Set up a monthly SIP in a Direct plan, and check that one fee number before anything else.**

Tomorrow: the tax you pay when you sell, and why waiting a few more months can make it smaller.

cards.body: Open your broker app and search 'Nifty 50 index fund'. Open two funds whose names include 'Direct' and write down each one's expense ratio. Circle the lower one. You don't have to invest a rupee tonight.
cards.simpler: Open your broker app and search for 'Nifty 50 index fund'. Open two funds that have 'Direct' in their names, and **write down each one's expense ratio**. Circle the lower one. That's the cheaper fund. You don't have to invest a single rupee tonight.
